stem: Match each deformity to the affected nerve.

items.left: Waiter's tip hand / Erb-Duchenne
Hand of benediction
Wrist drop
Ulnar Claw / Klumpke's paralysis

answer:
The pairings:

DeformityAffected nerve
Waiter's tip hand / Erb-DuchenneUpper brachial plexus injury
Hand of benedictionMedian nerve
Wrist dropRadial nerve
Ulnar Claw / Klumpke's paralysisUlnar nerve

Waiter's tip hand: Upper brachial plexus injury (C5-C6) → Erb-Duchenne palsy, the "waiter's tip" posture.

Hand of benediction: median nerve — the hand of benediction (inability to flex the index and middle fingers when attempting to make a fist).

Wrist drop: radial nerve — the radial nerve supplies the extensor compartment (Q15), so its loss drops the wrist.

Ulnar claw: ulnar nerve — the ulnar claw.

From Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus. The claw is the ulnar nerve's signature, from loss of the intrinsic hand muscles, and the lecture puts the ulnar nerve on the medial cord carrying C8 and T1 only - the inferior trunk. That shared root is the link to Klumpke's palsy: a lower plexus injury (C8-T1, classically after shoulder dystocia) takes out the ulnar supply at its origin and produces the same claw.

  • The radial nerve (posterior cord, C5-T1) gives wrist drop, not a claw.
  • The median nerve (all five roots) gives thenar weakness, not the ulnar claw.
  • The upper plexus (Erb's palsy, C5-C6) spares the hand.

flags.title: The option pairs two different lesions
flags.html: Klumpke's palsy is a lower brachial plexus injury (C8-T1), not an ulnar nerve lesion — though it produces a claw hand because the C8-T1 roots feed the ulnar nerve. Given that the option list offers no "lower brachial plexus" choice (only upper, which is Q61's answer), C is the intended answer, but do not carry away the idea that Klumpke's palsy is an ulnar neuropathy.

stem: Match each definition to the correct rotator cuff pathology.

items.left: This pathology is indicated by tendon inflammation without evidence of structural defect.
This pathology is defined as rotator cuff arthropathy.
This pathology is indicated by a partial thickness tear in the rotator cuff.
This pathology is indicated by a full thickness tear in the rotator cuff.

answer:
The pairings:

DefinitionRotator cuff pathology
This pathology is indicated by tendon inflammation without evidence of structural defect.Stage I rotator cuff disease
This pathology is defined as rotator cuff arthropathy.Stage IV rotator cuff disease
This pathology is indicated by a partial thickness tear in the rotator cuff.Stage II rotator cuff disease
This pathology is indicated by a full thickness tear in the rotator cuff.Stage III rotator cuff disease

Stage I: inflammation with no structural defect is the earliest stage.

Stage IV: From Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder. Rotator cuff disease is progressive, and the notes' spectrum ends in rotator cuff arthropathy: a massive cuff defect lets the humeral head migrate superiorly until it touches the acromion, and arthritis follows. That end stage is Stage IV in the workbook's scheme, and it is the stage treated by shoulder arthroplasty rather than cuff repair.

Stage II: Stage II is the first structural defect: a partial-thickness defect of the supraspinatus tendon at its articular end (not the bursal end) - the "mild tear". It follows from the lecture's intrinsic mechanism: vascularity is lost from the articular portion of the tendon distally, so that is where fibres fail first. Cuff repair is reserved for Stage II-III disease that fails conservative care.

Stage III: a full-thickness supraspinatus defect - the "severe tear". With the cuff no longer holding the head down, the humerus displaces superiorly and synovial fluid can leak into the surrounding tissue (swelling). It is still short of the massive defect and arthritis that define arthropathy. Stage I, by contrast, is intact but inflamed (the impingement stage, the one acromioplasty treats).

The workbook also offered a Stage V; there is no Stage V, and it was never used.

See rotator cuff tendinopathy.

stem: Match the common presentation to the pediatric condition.

items.left: A child (between 3-10 y.o) who was sick with a URTI about a week ago now has sudden unilateral hip pain and their hip is held in slight FABER position
An adolescent athlete (8-14 y.o female, 10-15 y.o male) has a painful bump over their tibial tuberosity and xray shows a teardrop sign.
An obese adolescent (~ 12 y.o female, 14 y.o male) has gradual left hip pain that refers to the knee, antalgic gait, and can’t weight bear
A child (between 4-8 y.o) who has a low body weight and protein S/C deficiency has gradual vague hip pain and stiffness and limb-length discrepancy

answer:
The pairings:

PresentationPediatric condition
A child (between 3-10 y.o) who was sick with a URTI about a week ago now has sudden unilateral hip pain and their hip is held in slight FABER positionTransient synovitis
An adolescent athlete (8-14 y.o female, 10-15 y.o male) has a painful bump over their tibial tuberosity and xray shows a teardrop sign.Osgood-Schlatter
An obese adolescent (~ 12 y.o female, 14 y.o male) has gradual left hip pain that refers to the knee, antalgic gait, and can’t weight bearSlipped capital femoral epiphysis
A child (between 4-8 y.o) who has a low body weight and protein S/C deficiency has gradual vague hip pain and stiffness and limb-length discrepancyLegg-Calve-Perthes

From 09 - Child with a Limp and 04 - Pediatric Orthopedics. Age plus one hallmark sorts each:

  • Transient synovitis: ages 3-10, a viral URTI 7-10 days earlier, sudden unilateral hip pain, the hip held flexed, abducted and externally rotated, afebrile.
  • Osgood-Schlatter: traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity in active 8-14 (F) / 10-15 (M) year olds; x-ray shows the "teardrop" sign.
  • SCFE: adolescent, gradual hip pain referred to the knee, left more often than right, painful weight-bearing.
  • Legg-Calve-Perthes: ages 4-8, low birth weight, gradual vague hip pain, stiffness and limb-length discrepancy from femoral-head osteonecrosis.

The stem's protein S/C deficiency is not in the note; its risk factors are family history, low birth weight and second-hand smoke.

stem: Match the clinical condition with neuronal structure affected.

items.left: Parkinson’s disease
Huntington’s disease
Schizophrenia

answer:
The pairings:

Clinical conditionStructure affected
Parkinson’s diseaseSubstantia Nigra
Huntington’s diseaseStriatum
SchizophreniaNucleus Accumbens

From 03 - Neuroanatomy of the Brainstem, Basal Ganglia, and Diencephalon. Each disease targets a different part of the dopamine and basal ganglia circuit.

  • Parkinson's → substantia nigra: the midbrain's dopamine-producing neurons are lost, the direct pathway becomes hypoactive, and thalamic output falls (bradykinesia).
  • Huntington's → striatum: the caudate and putamen degenerate, the indirect pathway goes quiet, and thalamic output rises (a hyperkinetic disorder).
  • Schizophrenia → nucleus accumbens: the accumbens is the ventral striatum, a limbic dopamine target. 07 - Introduction to Psychopharmacology ties positive symptoms to excess dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway.

The trap is that the accumbens is also striatum. Huntington's is a movement disorder of the dorsal striatum (caudate and putamen).

stem: Match the correct location of decussation to each of the following tracts.

items.left: Corticospinal
Spinothalamic
Medial lemniscus

answer:
The pairings:

TractLocation of decussation
CorticospinalMedulla
SpinothalamicSpinal cord entry
Medial lemniscusMedulla

From 04 - Neuroanatomy of the Spinal Tracts and Cerebellum. Two of the three long tracts cross in the medulla. Only the pain pathway crosses as soon as it enters the cord.

  • Corticospinal → medulla: 90% of axons cross at the pyramidal decussation into the lateral corticospinal tract. The other 10% stay ipsilateral in the anterior tract.
  • Medial lemniscus → medulla: the second-order neurons in the nucleus gracilis and cuneatus send their axons across as the medial lemniscus.
  • Spinothalamic → spinal cord entry: the first-order neuron synapses in the dorsal horn at once, and the second-order axon crosses in the anterior white commissure.

This split is why a hemicord (Brown-Séquard) lesion causes ipsilateral loss of vibration and proprioception but contralateral loss of pain and temperature.
note: HippoNotes prose key "Medulla: Corticospinal, Medial lemniscus; Spinal cord entry: Spinothalamic"

items.left: Schatzki ring (an intermittent dysphagia)
Jackhammer esophagus (an intermittent dysphagia with chest pain and repetitive peristaltic contractions)

items.left: Scleroderma (a progressive dysphagia with heartburn)
items.right: Motility - issue with solids and liquids

items.left: Eosinophilic esophagitis (a dysphagia presenting with corrugate rings, vertical furrowing, white papules often in young males)
Diffuse spasms (a “corkscrew” esophagus on barium swallow)
items.right: Motility - issue with solids and liquids

items.left: Achalasia (a “bird’s beak” on barium swallowing often with regurgitation of bland food)

answer:
The pairings:

DysphagiaType
Schatzki ring (an intermittent dysphagia)Mechanical - issue with solids only
Jackhammer esophagus (an intermittent dysphagia with chest pain and repetitive peristaltic contractions)Motility - issue with solids and liquids
Scleroderma (a progressive dysphagia with heartburn)Motility - issue with solids and liquids
Eosinophilic esophagitis (a dysphagia presenting with corrugate rings, vertical furrowing, white papules often in young males)Mechanical - issue with solids only
Diffuse spasms (a “corkscrew” esophagus on barium swallow)Motility - issue with solids and liquids

From 04 - Esophageal Dysphagia (PoM 1, Gastroenterology Week 10). This question is GI, not psychiatry. The first history question is whether solids alone get stuck, or both solids and liquids. A fixed narrowing blocks only solids, while a motility failure affects both.

  • Mechanical: Schatzki ring, eosinophilic esophagitis. A Schatzki ring is a distal mucosal ring that causes intermittent solid-food dysphagia. Eosinophilic esophagitis (rings, vertical furrows, food bolus impaction in young atopic males) is grouped with the structural causes.
  • Motility: jackhammer, scleroderma, diffuse spasm, achalasia. Jackhammer esophagus (high-amplitude repetitive contractions), scleroderma (scarred, thickened wall), diffuse esophageal spasm (simultaneous non-propulsive contractions, the corkscrew) and achalasia (the LES fails to relax, the bird's beak).

Motility disorders are diagnosed by manometry, not endoscopy.

DescriptionPsychotherapy

From 10 - Psychotherapies in Mood and Anxiety Disorders. Each description names a feature that only one therapy has:

  • Psychodynamic: unstructured free association, a neutral “blank screen” therapist, interpretation of transference, and defences worked through by clarifying and confronting.
  • DBT: developed specifically for borderline personality disorder. It uses behavioural chain analysis and is delivered as individual therapy, group skills training, phone coaching and therapist consultation.
  • CBT: schemas, automatic thoughts and cognitive distortions, tracked with thought records.
  • Behavioural activation: act before you feel better, using activity scheduling rated for accomplishment and pleasure.
  • IPT: short, present-focused work on role disputes, role transitions, grief and interpersonal deficits. Transference is deliberately not addressed, which is the clearest contrast with psychodynamic therapy.

stem: Match the term to the correct description.

items.left: Where vivid dreaming occurs and may be important for memory consolidation. EEG shows low-voltage fast waves, muscle atonia and rapid eye movements. Sawtooth wave form, theta activity and slow alpha activity.
Transitional role in sleep-stage cycle. EEG shows transitions from wakefulness (rhythmic alpha waves) to low-voltage, mixed frequency waves.
Related to memory consolidation. EGG shows low voltage fast activity characterized by the presence of sleep spindles and K-complexes.
Primary function is daily brain recovery and secretion of growth hormone is greatest during this stage. EEG shows high voltage, slow-wave activity, large delta waves.

answer:
The pairings:

DescriptionSleep stage
Where vivid dreaming occurs and may be important for memory consolidation. EEG shows low-voltage fast waves, muscle atonia and rapid eye movements. Sawtooth wave form, theta activity and slow alpha activity.REM Sleep
Transitional role in sleep-stage cycle. EEG shows transitions from wakefulness (rhythmic alpha waves) to low-voltage, mixed frequency waves.N1 Sleep
Related to memory consolidation. EGG shows low voltage fast activity characterized by the presence of sleep spindles and K-complexes.N2 Sleep
Primary function is daily brain recovery and secretion of growth hormone is greatest during this stage. EEG shows high voltage, slow-wave activity, large delta waves.N3 Sleep

From 01 - Sleep Disorders. Match each EEG signature to its stage:

  • REM: low-voltage fast activity with sawtooth waves, plus vivid dreaming, muscle atonia and rapid eye movements. It is thought to help memory consolidation.
  • N1: the transition from wakefulness, as alpha waves give way to low-voltage mixed-frequency (theta) waves. Only 2-5% of sleep, and easily interrupted.
  • N2: sleep spindles and K-complexes, linked to memory consolidation. At 45-55% of sleep, it is the largest share.
  • N3: high-voltage slow (delta) waves, daily brain recovery and growth hormone secretion. It is the hardest stage to wake from and is concentrated in the first third of the night.

Anchor each stage on one unique feature: alpha to theta (N1), spindles (N2), delta (N3), sawtooth (REM).

items.left: Angleman syndrome

SyndromeBehavioural phenotype
Angleman syndromeJerky movement
Williams syndromeHyperverbalisation
Prader-Willi syndromeNeonatal hypotonia

From 09 - Autism Spectrum Disorder & Intellectual Disabilities and the syndrome notes. Each genetic cause of intellectual disability has a recognisable behavioural phenotype:

  • Angelman → jerky movement: ataxic movement with a characteristically happy demeanour.
  • Williams → hyperverbalisation: an overfriendly, talkative child whose verbal fluency outruns their cognition.
  • Prader-Willi → neonatal hypotonia: a floppy newborn.
  • Fragile X → anxiety and agitation: social anxiety is prominent. Fragile X is the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability.

From 08 - Developmental Milestones (FoM Block 1, Week 3). The lecture's red-flag list gives most of these directly:

  • Not walking = 18 mo: most walk independently by 12 mo; the red flag is not walking by 18 mo.
  • Hands still fisted = 4 mo: the palmar grasp reflex fades by 3-4 mo.
  • No babbling = 9 mo: babbling a series of sounds (baba, duhduh) is the 9-month language milestone.
  • No joint attention = 15 mo: the lecture's flag is not pointing to objects of interest by 15 mo, which is joint attention.
